learnings.title: The RADIO framework — the spine of every answer
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
An unstructured system design answer fails for a reason that has nothing to do with knowledge: the interviewer cannot tell whether you covered something or forgot it. **RADIO** is the five-stage spine that makes your coverage legible — to them and to you. > **R**equirements · **A**rchitecture · **D**ata model · **I**nterface · **O**ptimisations ## The five stages ```mermaid flowchart LR R["Requirements
what are we building"] --> A["Architecture
what are the pieces"] A --> D["Data model
what does each piece hold"] D --> I["Interface
how do they talk"] I --> O["Optimisations
what breaks at scale"] ``` Every stage answers one question, and each one is useless before the one above it is settled. You cannot draw components before you know what the product does; you cannot design an API before you know what data crosses the boundary. ### R — Requirements (5–8 min) Split them in two, out loud, because interviewers grade the split: | Functional | Non-functional | | --- | --- | | What a user can *do* | What the system must *be* | | "Post a comment, see replies, edit within 5 minutes" | "Readable in under 1s on 3G, works offline, WCAG AA, 40 languages" | Then **state the scope you are cutting**. "I'm going to design the feed read path and leave posting, moderation and notifications out unless you'd rather I cover those" is one sentence that buys you the whole rest of the interview. ### A — Architecture (8–12 min) The component diagram, and the *boundaries* between components. For a frontend this means: the rendering strategy, where state lives, what the client owns versus the BFF, and which pieces are lazily loaded. Name each box and say what it owns. Boxes with no stated responsibility are the most common way to look busy while saying nothing. ### D — Data model (5–8 min) Not database tables — **the shapes the client holds**. What does one `Post` look like in the store? Is it normalised by id, or a nested tree? Who owns `unreadCount`, the server or the client? ```javascript // Normalised: one copy of each entity, lists hold ids { posts: { 'p1': { id: 'p1', authorId: 'u9', body: '…', likeCount: 12 } }, users: { 'u9': { id: 'u9', name: 'Ada' } }, feed: { ids: ['p1', 'p2'], cursor: 'eyJ…', status: 'ready' }, } ``` Say why. Normalised means a like on one screen updates every screen showing that post; nested means it does not. ### I — Interface (5–8 min) Two interfaces, and juniors only mention one: 1. **Network** — the API contract. Endpoints, shapes, pagination style, error shape. 2. **Component** — the props and callbacks between your own components. This is the half that makes it a *frontend* interview. ```javascript // Network GET /feed?cursor=&limit=20 → { items: Post[], nextCursor: string | null } // Component void} onLike={(postId: string) => void} state="loading" | "ready" | "error" | "empty" /> ``` ### O — Optimisations (10–15 min) The stage that separates levels, and the one people run out of clock for. Performance, accessibility, error states, offline, i18n, security, observability. **Budget for it deliberately** — see the 45-minute clock entry. ## Using it without sounding like a script Say the stage name once when you enter it — "OK, I've got the requirements, let me sketch the architecture" — and then talk normally. The signposting is for their notes, not for their entertainment. ## Common mistakes - **Starting at A.** Drawing boxes in minute two. You are now designing something nobody agreed to. - **Treating R as a formality.** Asking three questions, getting three answers, ignoring all of them for the next forty minutes. - **Skipping D entirely** because "it's a frontend interview". The client data model *is* the frontend design. - **Letting O be whatever time is left.** It is the highest-signal stage; protect it. ## Key takeaways - RADIO is a coverage checklist, not a script — it makes your completeness visible. - Requirements come in two kinds and you must say both kinds out loud. - Interface means the network contract *and* the component contract. - Optimisations is where senior signal lives, so it gets protected time. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Where would you start if I gave you only 20 minutes?"** — R and A in full, D compressed to the one entity that matters, then jump to the two optimisations with the highest impact for this product. - **"You skipped the data model."** — The honest recovery is "you're right, let me do that now" — not defending the omission.

learnings.title: The 45-minute clock — timeboxing and what to say out loud
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Most failed system design rounds are not failures of knowledge. They are **clock failures**: thirty minutes on requirements and component boxes, then a panicked two-minute gallop through performance while the interviewer writes "did not reach depth".

Design the interview like you would design the system: with a budget.

## The 45-minute budget

| Minutes | Stage | You should have on the board |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–2 | Framing | The one-sentence restatement + your plan for the hour |
| 2–9 | Requirements | Functional list, non-functional list, explicit out-of-scope |
| 9–20 | Architecture | Component diagram, rendering strategy, state topology |
| 20–26 | Data model | The 2–3 entity shapes the client holds |
| 26–33 | Interface | API contract + the top-level component API |
| 33–43 | Optimisations | Perf, a11y, errors, offline — *the deep-dive stage* |
| 43–45 | Wrap | What you'd do next, what you traded away |

A 60-minute round is the same shape with optimisations at 20 minutes instead of 10. The extra time is **always** for depth, never for more breadth.

## The two-minute opening, verbatim

> "So — a news feed for a social product. Before I design anything I want to pin down scope, because 'feed' could mean the read path, the composer, ranking, or all three. I'll spend about five minutes on requirements, ten on architecture and state, then I want to leave a solid ten minutes at the end for performance and accessibility, because at feed scale that's where the interesting decisions are. Does that split work for you?"

That paragraph does four things: restates the problem, flags the ambiguity, states your budget, and hands them a chance to redirect you before you have spent anything.

## What to say at each transition

Narration is the whole game in a system design round. The interviewer is scoring what they *hear you consider*, not what is in your head.

| Moment | Say this |
| --- | --- |
| Entering architecture | "I'll sketch the pieces first, then come back and justify the rendering choice." |
| Making any choice | "I'm picking X over Y because ___. If ___ changed, I'd switch to Y." |
| Hitting something you don't know | "I haven't worked with that directly — my instinct is ___, and I'd verify it by ___." |
| Realising you're wrong | "Actually, that doesn't hold — if ___ then ___. Let me redo that bit." |
| Running long | "I'm about ten minutes from the end and I want to make sure I cover performance. Shall I move on, or is this branch more interesting?" |

That last one is a **senior move**. Managing the clock collaboratively reads as someone who runs meetings well.

## The trade-off sentence

Every choice you make should come out in this shape:

> "I'd use **\<choice\>** because **\<what it optimises\>**, accepting **\<what it costs\>**. The thing that would change my mind is **\<condition\>**."

Concrete:

> "I'd use cursor pagination because offset pagination duplicates and skips items when the feed mutates under you, accepting that the reader can't jump to page 40. If this were an admin table with stable data and a page picker, offset would be the right call."

Say three sentences in that shape across the interview and you have demonstrated judgement, which is the thing actually being tested.

## The last two minutes

Do not trail off. Close deliberately:

> "To recap: SSR shell for first paint, cursor-paginated feed, normalised client store, optimistic likes with rollback. If I had more time I'd go deeper on the offline story and on how ranking changes the caching. The main thing I traded away was ___, and I'd revisit that if ___."

## Common mistakes

- **No opening plan.** You lose the chance to have the interviewer correct your scope while it is still cheap.
- **Silent thinking.** Ten seconds of silence is fine. Sixty is an unscored minute.
- **Answering the question you wish they asked.** If they steer you to caching, go to caching.
- **Defending a choice under pushback instead of pricing it.** They are usually testing whether you know the cost, not whether you will fold.

## Key takeaways

- Budget the interview out loud in the first two minutes, and protect the optimisations block.
- Narrate transitions and choices; unspoken reasoning scores zero.
- Use the trade-off sentence shape — choice, benefit, cost, what would change it.
- Close with a deliberate recap rather than running out of time.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"We're running short — pick the most important thing left."** — Name it and say why it's the most important, then do it. The reasoning is the answer.
- **"You've been on requirements a while."** — That is a redirect, not a comment. Move immediately.

learnings.title: What interviewers actually grade — the signal rubric by level
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Interviewers do not score "was the design good". They fill in a rubric, usually four to six dimensions, and then argue for a level. Knowing the dimensions tells you where to spend effort.

## The dimensions

| Dimension | What a weak answer looks like | What a strong answer looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Scoping** | Starts designing immediately | Separates functional from non-functional, names what is out of scope |
| **Breadth** | Only covers components | Rendering, state, network, caching, perf, a11y, errors, security |
| **Depth** | Every topic gets one sentence | Goes three levels down on at least two topics unprompted |
| **Trade-offs** | "I'd use GraphQL" | "GraphQL because ___, costing ___, and I'd use REST instead if ___" |
| **Frontend specificity** | Describes a backend | Talks about hydration, bundle budget, layout shift, focus management |
| **Communication** | Silent, or rambling | Signposts, narrates, checks in, recovers from mistakes cleanly |

**Frontend specificity** is the one candidates lose most often and notice least. A design that would be identical if the client were a CLI is not a frontend design.

## The level ladder

The same answer maps to different levels depending on *how* it is reached.

### SDE2 / Mid

- Covers the stages when prompted
- Names the right technologies
- Handles the happy path completely
- **Gap:** waits to be asked about errors, a11y, and failure modes

> "I'd fetch the feed and render the list. Pagination with a cursor." — correct, and complete only for the happy path.

### Senior

- Covers the stages **unprompted**
- Every significant choice arrives with its cost
- Raises failure modes before being asked
- Connects decisions to product consequences
- **Gap:** designs the system, not the system's evolution

> "Cursor pagination, and I want to talk about what happens when the feed mutates between pages — with offset you get duplicates, so cursor isn't just neater, it's correctness. Empty, error and end-of-feed all need states; the end state is the one people forget."

### Staff

Everything above, plus:

- **Names the constraint that actually drives the design.** "The whole design turns on whether ranking is personalised. If it is, nothing is cacheable at the edge and this becomes a different problem."
- **Designs for change.** "I'd keep the ranking behind the BFF so the client never learns the shape of it — that's the part most likely to be rewritten."
- **Talks about people.** Ownership boundaries, how three teams ship into this without stepping on each other, what the migration path looks like.
- **Prices the organisation, not just the request.** "Micro-frontends would solve the deploy coupling, but it costs you a shared design system, a routing contract, and roughly one full-time person. Under about four teams I would not pay that."

## The two-question test

At the end, the interviewer is really asking themselves two things:

1. **Would I want this person on my team's design review?**
2. **Did they show me something I hadn't thought of?**

Answer two gets you the level bump. Deep-diving one topic further than required — *unprompted* — is the most reliable way to trigger it.

## Where points are silently lost

- **Not saying the cost.** A choice with no stated cost reads as a preference, not a decision.
- **Accessibility as an afterthought.** One sentence at minute 44 scores lower than nothing, because it signals you know it matters and chose not to design for it.
- **Perfect breadth, zero depth.** Ten topics at one sentence each reads as a checklist recital. Two topics at four levels deep reads as experience.
- **Being right but unclear.** If they cannot follow it, it did not happen.

## Key takeaways

- You are scored on dimensions, and frontend specificity is the one most often missed.
- Senior is where costs arrive unprompted; Staff is where you name the driving constraint and design for change.
- Depth on two topics beats breadth on ten.
- Aim to say one thing the interviewer had not considered.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Anything you'd change?"** — Not a trap. Name a real trade-off you made and the condition that would flip it.
- **"How would you convince a teammate who disagreed?"** — They are testing whether your reasoning survives contact with a peer. Argue from the constraint, not from preference.

learnings.title: Startup vs MNC vs FAANG — what each round optimises for
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The same prompt — "design a dashboard" — is scored against three different rubrics depending on who is asking. Reading the room is not a soft skill here; it changes which answer is correct.

## The three shapes

| | Startup (seed–Series B) | MNC / product company | FAANG-tier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Round length** | 30–45 min, often ad hoc | 45–60 min, structured | 45–60 min, calibrated rubric |
| **Interviewer** | A founder or the first FE hire | Your future tech lead | A trained interviewer, often from another org |
| **Really asking** | "Can you ship this alone next month?" | "Can you own this area and mentor?" | "Do you reason at the level we're hiring for?" |
| **Rewards** | Pragmatism, speed, scope-cutting | Maintainability, team fit, ownership | Depth, trade-off rigour, scale reasoning |
| **Punishes** | Over-engineering | Hand-waving the hard parts | Breadth without depth |
| **Scale framing** | "10k users and we'd be thrilled" | "500k users, 30 engineers" | "100M users, assume it matters" |

## What changes in your answer

### Startup

Lead with **what you would not build**.

> "For a seed-stage product I'd put this on Next.js with server components, use the hosted auth provider, and not build a design system — just Tailwind plus five shared components. The whole thing is one repo, one deploy. I'd revisit that at the point where a second frontend team exists."

Saying "we don't need Redux, this is four screens" scores *higher* here than a correct description of Redux. Naming the cost of complexity in **weeks of one engineer's time** is the currency.

The killer question is always some form of *"how fast can you get something in front of users?"* Have a real answer: what ships in week one, what ships in month one, and what you deliberately defer.

### MNC / product company

Lead with **boundaries and ownership**.

> "I'd split this into three feature modules with an owner each, and put the shared pieces behind a versioned design system package. The contract between the modules is a routing manifest plus a shared event bus, so a team can deploy without coordinating."

They are hiring someone who will still be maintaining this in three years, next to people who will join and leave. Testing strategy, code review norms, migration paths, how a junior finds their way in — all of this is on-topic and often decisive. "How would you onboard someone onto this codebase?" is a real question here.

### FAANG-tier

Lead with **the constraint and the numbers**.

> "At 100M DAU the feed can't be personalised at the edge, so I need to split the response: a cacheable shell the CDN can serve to everyone, and a small personalised overlay fetched separately. That turns one uncacheable request into one 30ms edge hit plus one 80ms personalised call."

Expect the interviewer to pick one branch and push until you reach the edge of what you know. **That is the point of the round**, not a sign it is going badly. Going four levels deep on hydration, or on why `content-visibility` helps but `will-change` hurts, is exactly the signal.

Do the arithmetic out loud. 100k requests/sec, 2 kB per item, 20 items — that is 4 GB/s and it changes the design. Interviewers at this tier are explicitly told to look for whether you quantify.

## Reading which room you are in

You usually can, within five minutes:

- They say "we" about the product and mention next quarter → **startup**
- They describe the team and the surrounding services → **MNC**
- They give you an abstract prompt and a scale number → **FAANG-tier**

And you are allowed to just ask: *"Should I design this for where you are now, or for where you're heading?"* The answer tells you which rubric you are on, and asking scores well in all three.

## Common mistakes

- **One rehearsed answer for every company.** The FAANG answer at a seed startup reads as someone who will gold-plate everything.
- **Under-designing at FAANG.** "I'd keep it simple" without engaging the scale number reads as not understanding the scale number.
- **Ignoring the team at an MNC.** A beautiful architecture with no ownership story misses what they are hiring for.

## Key takeaways

- Startups buy speed and scope-cutting; MNCs buy maintainability and ownership; FAANG buys depth and quantified trade-offs.
- Lead with what you would *not* build at a startup, boundaries at an MNC, the driving constraint at FAANG.
- Ask which one you are designing for — it is a legitimate scoping question.
- Being pushed deep is the round working, not the round failing.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"What would you do differently with 10× the users?"** — Name the first thing that breaks, then the second. Two named failure points beats a general answer.
- **"What would you cut to ship in two weeks?"** — Cut features, never correctness. Cutting the error states is the wrong answer at every tier.

learnings.title: Frontend vs backend system design — what is actually different
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Candidates who have prepared with backend system design material walk in and describe shards, replicas and message queues — for a UI. The frameworks rhyme, but almost every specific is different, because the two disciplines optimise against different constraints.

## The constraint is different

Backend system design is fundamentally about **a shared resource under contention**: many clients, finite servers, consistency across replicas.

Frontend system design is about **one hostile, untrusted, wildly variable execution environment**: one device, one network, one user, and you control none of them.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph BE["Backend: scale out"]
    B1["More load → add machines"]
    B2["Bottleneck: throughput, consistency"]
  end
  subgraph FE["Frontend: one device"]
    F1["More load → the same phone, slower"]
    F2["Bottleneck: main thread, bandwidth, memory"]
  end
```

You cannot horizontally scale a user's phone. Every byte you ship is spent on a device you did not choose, over a network you cannot predict.

## The translation table

| Backend concept | Frontend equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Horizontal scaling | Code splitting and lazy loading — you cannot add devices, only ship less to the one you have |
| Load balancing | The CDN, plus which work goes to server vs client vs worker |
| Database sharding | IndexedDB, Cache Storage, and what you are allowed to keep on the device |
| Replication lag | Stale client cache — the same problem, and you own the invalidation |
| Rate limiting | Debounce, throttle, request cancellation, `AbortController` |
| Circuit breaker | Error boundaries, retry with backoff, graceful degradation to a cached view |
| Message queue | The event loop, the microtask queue, `scheduler.postTask` |
| Idempotency keys | Still idempotency keys — this one survives intact, and you need it for retried mutations |
| Monitoring / APM | RUM, Core Web Vitals, error tracking, session replay |
| Consistency model | Optimistic updates, conflict resolution, CRDTs |

## What has no backend analogue at all

These are the topics that make it a *frontend* interview, and skipping them is the most common way to fail one:

1. **Rendering strategy.** CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming, islands. There is no server-side equivalent of choosing when HTML becomes readable.
2. **Hydration.** Shipping the markup twice — once as HTML, once as the JS that re-attaches to it — is a uniquely frontend cost.
3. **The main thread.** One thread renders, runs your JS, and handles input. A 200 ms task is a 200 ms freeze. Backends have thread pools; you have a Web Worker and a lot of care.
4. **Layout and paint.** Reflow, repaint, compositing, cumulative layout shift. Reading `offsetHeight` after a style write is a performance bug with no backend equivalent.
5. **Accessibility.** The accessibility tree, focus management, screen reader semantics, keyboard traps. Non-optional and frequently legally required.
6. **Bundle budget.** Every dependency is paid for by every user on every cold load, forever.
7. **The browser is the attacker's machine.** XSS, CSP, and the rule that nothing on the client can be trusted or kept secret.

## What genuinely carries over

- **Caching and invalidation** — the layers differ, the hard part is identical.
- **Pagination** — cursor beats offset for the same reason in both places.
- **Idempotency** — a retried POST must not double-charge, wherever the retry originates.
- **Backpressure** — a client that fires a request per keystroke is a client DoSing your API.
- **Observability** — you cannot fix what you cannot see, on either side.

## Where the interview actually meets the backend

You *will* be asked about the API contract, and "that's the backend's problem" is a failing answer. The frontend-correct framing is to design the contract **from the UI's needs backwards**:

> "The screen needs post, author and the viewer's like state together — so I want one endpoint that returns them joined, not three that the client has to stitch. If the backend can't do that, I'd put a BFF in front, because otherwise every screen pays three round trips and I've moved their join into the user's latency budget."

That is a frontend answer about a backend boundary, and it is exactly the signal they are looking for.

## Common mistakes

- **Describing a backend.** If your design would be unchanged with a CLI client, you have not done the exercise.
- **Ignoring the device.** No mention of bundle size, main thread, or what happens on a mid-range Android on 4G.
- **"That's the backend's job."** The API contract is a shared design surface and you are expected to have opinions about it.
- **Accessibility and error states as an appendix.** They are architecture, not polish.

## Key takeaways

- Backend scales out; the frontend has one device it cannot scale, so the lever is shipping less.
- Many concepts translate — caching, pagination, idempotency, backpressure — but rendering, hydration, the main thread, layout, a11y and bundle budget have no analogue.
- Design the API contract backwards from what the screen needs.
- A design that would work identically for a CLI is not a frontend design.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Where would you put this logic, client or server?"** — Answer with the constraint: anything that must be trusted, anything that would ship a large dependency, and anything needed for first paint goes server-side.
- **"How is this different from designing the backend for it?"** — A direct invitation to name the main thread, the bundle, and the rendering strategy.

learnings.title: Walking through a system you have built
learnings.answer:
Round 2 often asks you to walk through a **real frontend system** you've built — modules, component hierarchy, APIs, caching, and **non-functional requirements** (latency, availability). Use a structured template so you don't ramble.

## Interview template (STAR + architecture)

### 1. Context (30 seconds)

- Product, users, scale (DAU, requests/day, team size)
- Your role and boundaries

### 2. High-level architecture

```
Browser (SPA)
├── Shell / routing (React Router)
├── Feature modules (lazy-loaded)
│   ├── Dashboard
│   ├── Settings
│   └── Reports
├── Shared design system
├── API client layer (fetch + interceptors)
├── State (server cache + local UI state)
└── Observability (RUM, error tracking)
        ↓
    BFF / REST / GraphQL
        ↓
    Backend services
```

### 3. Component hierarchy (example)

- **App** → **Layout** → **Feature pages** → **containers** (data) → **presentational** components
- Colocate hooks with features; shared primitives in design system

### 4. API contracts

| Concern | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Shape | REST resources or GraphQL schema shared via OpenAPI/ codegen |
| Errors | Consistent `{ code, message, details }` envelope |
| Auth | Short-lived access token + refresh; attach in interceptor |
| Versioning | URL or header versioning for breaking changes |

### 5. Caching strategy

| Layer | Tool | Use case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP | `Cache-Control`, ETag | Static assets, idempotent GETs |
| Client data | React Query / SWR | Stale-while-revalidate, dedupe in-flight |
| Local | IndexedDB / localStorage | Offline drafts, user prefs |
| CDN | Edge cache | JS bundles, images |

### 6. Non-functional requirements

| NFR | Tactics |
| --- | --- |
| **Response time** | Code splitting, prefetch, skeleton UI, p95 budgets |
| **Availability** | Error boundaries, graceful degradation, retry with backoff |
| **Security** | CSP, sanitize HTML, no secrets in client bundle |
| **Accessibility** | Semantic HTML, keyboard flows, CI a11y checks |

### 7. Tradeoffs you made

- Why SPA vs SSR (SEO, TTFB, interactivity)
- Global state vs server cache (React Query reduced Redux surface)
- Monorepo design system vs per-app duplication

## How to answer in the interview

> "I'll describe [product] at [scale]. Architecturally it's a lazy-loaded SPA with a shared design system and an API client layer. We used React Query for server state with stale-while-revalidate. Non-functionally we targeted p95 < 300ms for critical paths, error boundaries for availability, and Sentry for client errors. Key tradeoff: we chose CSR over SSR because…"

## Common mistakes

- Diving into code before stating context and scale
- Ignoring NFRs until interviewer prompts
- No concrete metrics or outcomes

## Key takeaways

- Use a **template**: context → diagram → modules → APIs → cache → NFRs → tradeoffs.
- Name **tools and why**, not buzzwords only.
- Quantify impact where possible (LCP, error rate, bundle size).

## Interview follow-ups

- **How handle auth token refresh?** — Interceptor queue requests during refresh.
- **How deploy without downtime?** — Blue/green or canary; cache-busted asset URLs.

learnings.title: Functional vs non-functional requirements for a frontend
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The first five minutes decide the other forty. Requirements come in two kinds, and interviewers grade you on whether you separate them — because engineers who do not separate them build the right features with the wrong properties.

## The split

**Functional** = what a user can *do*. Verbs. Testable by clicking.
**Non-functional** = what the system must *be*. Adjectives. Testable by measuring.

For "design a comment thread":

| Functional | Non-functional |
| --- | --- |
| Post a comment | First comment readable within 1.5s on 4G |
| Reply to a comment, nested to 3 levels | Works with keyboard only, WCAG 2.1 AA |
| Edit within 5 minutes of posting | Survives losing connectivity mid-compose |
| React with an emoji | Renders 10,000 comments without jank |
| Load more as you scroll | Available in 12 locales, incl. RTL |

Note how the non-functional column is what actually makes this hard. Anyone can render a list of comments. Rendering 10,000 of them, on a mid-range Android, for a screen reader user, in Arabic, while offline — that is the design problem.

## The frontend non-functional checklist

Backend candidates say "availability, latency, consistency". The frontend list is different, and reciting it separates you immediately:

| Category | The question to ask | A concrete target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Performance** | How fast on what device and network? | LCP < 2.5s at p75 on 4G / mid-tier Android |
| **Responsiveness** | How fast does it react to input? | INP < 200ms |
| **Stability** | Does it move under the reader? | CLS < 0.1 |
| **Accessibility** | Which standard, verified how? | WCAG 2.1 AA, keyboard + screen reader tested |
| **Reach** | Which browsers and devices? | Last 2 versions + Safari iOS 15, no IE |
| **Connectivity** | What happens offline or on a flaky link? | Reads from cache, writes queue and retry |
| **Internationalisation** | How many locales, any RTL? | 12 locales, Arabic and Hebrew RTL |
| **Security** | What is the threat model? | User-generated HTML → sanitise, strict CSP |
| **Observability** | How do we know it broke for a user? | RUM p75 vitals, error tracking with release tags |
| **Scale** | Scale of *what*, exactly? | 10k comments per thread, 200 concurrent editors |

## Make them numeric

"Fast" is not a requirement; it is a wish. Push for a number, or propose one and get it confirmed:

> "You said it should feel fast — can I take that as LCP under 2.5 seconds at p75, measured on a mid-range Android over 4G? If most of your traffic is desktop on good connections, I'd design this differently."

Now every later decision has something to be judged against. When you say "that pushes us over budget", it means something.

## Scale means different things on the frontend

"One million users" often changes *nothing* about a frontend design — they do not share a device. Ask what scales **per user**:

- How many items on one screen? (10 vs 10,000 decides virtualization)
- How large is one item's payload? (drives pagination size and image strategy)
- How often does it change? (drives the transport — polling vs SSE vs WebSocket)
- How many concurrent editors on one document? (decides whether you need CRDTs)

> "A million DAU doesn't change my client design much — they're on separate devices. What I do need to know is how many comments land in one thread, because 50 and 50,000 are different architectures."

That sentence alone is a strong signal.

## State what is out of scope

Requirements gathering ends with an explicit cut:

> "So: I'm designing the read and compose paths for a single thread. I'm treating moderation, notifications, and the ranking algorithm as out of scope — tell me if you'd rather I spend the time there instead."

This protects your clock and demonstrates scope management. It also gives the interviewer a cheap opportunity to redirect you before you have invested anything.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking questions and then ignoring the answers.** If they said "offline matters", offline must appear in the architecture.
- **"Fast", "scalable", "responsive".** Unmeasurable words. Convert them or drop them.
- **Reciting backend NFRs.** Availability and partition tolerance are rarely the frontend's design drivers.
- **No explicit out-of-scope.** You will run out of clock and it will look like you ran out of ideas.

## Key takeaways

- Functional is verbs, non-functional is adjectives — and the adjectives are where the design difficulty lives.
- The frontend NFR list is its own list: vitals, a11y, reach, connectivity, i18n, security, observability.
- Convert every vague adjective into a number you can design against.
- On the frontend, ask what scales *per user*, not how many users there are.
- Close requirements with an explicit statement of what you are not building.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Which requirement is hardest?"** — Name one and say why, in terms of what it rules out. "Offline is hardest, because it turns every mutation into a queued, idempotent, conflict-resolvable operation."
- **"What if we dropped the accessibility requirement?"** — Usually a values test. The honest answer is that focus management and semantics are cheap when designed in and expensive when retrofitted.

learnings.title: The clarifying-question bank
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
You get roughly five minutes and maybe six questions. Asking the wrong six makes you look like you are stalling; asking the right six reshapes the design. These are the questions that actually change what you build.

## The six that always earn their place

1. **"Who uses this, and on what?"**
   Consumer mobile web, internal desktop tool, and embedded partner widget are three different architectures. An internal admin tool on company laptops does not need SSR or a 100 kB budget.

2. **"What's the one thing that must feel instant?"**
   Every product has one. For search it is the typeahead; for a feed it is the first screen; for a checkout it is the payment confirmation. This tells you where to spend the entire performance budget.

3. **"How much data is on one screen, and how often does it change?"**
   Size decides virtualization and pagination. Change frequency decides the transport. These two numbers determine more of the design than anything else you can ask.

4. **"Is this read-heavy or write-heavy?"**
   Read-heavy → caching, prefetch, static rendering. Write-heavy → optimistic updates, conflict resolution, offline queue, idempotency.

5. **"Who else is editing the same thing at the same time?"**
   Nobody → simple. One other person occasionally → last-write-wins plus a warning. Many, simultaneously → OT or CRDT, and that is now the centre of the design.

6. **"What should happen when the network is bad or gone?"**
   The answer ranges from "show an error" to "fully offline with background sync", and the distance between those is most of your architecture.

## Per-problem extras

### Feeds and lists
- Is the order chronological or ranked? *(Ranked kills edge caching of the personalised part.)*
- Can items change after you have scrolled past them?
- Infinite scroll or pagination? Does anyone need to deep-link to item 400?

### Search and typeahead
- How fast must suggestions appear? Are stale results acceptable?
- Search-as-you-type or on submit? *(Decides whether you need cancellation.)*
- Does the result set need to be shareable as a URL?

### Editors and collaborative tools
- Plain text, rich text, or structured? *(Rich text is an order of magnitude more work.)*
- How many concurrent editors, realistically?
- Is edit history or undo across sessions required?

### Dashboards
- How fresh must the numbers be? *(Every second, every minute, and on-demand are three designs.)*
- How many charts render at once, and on what data volume?
- Can users build their own views, or are the layouts fixed?

### Media
- Who uploads, and how big? *(Decides chunked/resumable upload.)*
- Adaptive bitrate, or one file? DRM?
- Must it work on a poor connection?

## How to ask

Ask in a bundle, not one at a time, and offer your own assumption so silence still moves you forward:

> "Three quick ones. First, is this mobile-web-first or desktop? Second, is the feed ranked or chronological? Third, how many items in a typical session — tens or thousands? I'll assume mobile-first, ranked, and a few hundred unless you say otherwise."

That is efficient, it shows you know which variables matter, and it gets you moving even if they say "you decide".

## Questions that waste your five minutes

- **"What's the tech stack?"** — You are being asked to choose it. Pick one and justify it.
- **"How many users?"** — Rarely changes a frontend design on its own. Ask what scales per user instead.
- **"What's the team size?"** — Only relevant if you are about to propose micro-frontends or a shared design system. Ask it there, not up front.
- **Anything you will not act on.** If the answer would not change your design, do not spend a question on it.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for permission instead of information.** "Should I use React?" is not a clarifying question.
- **Not stating a default.** "You decide" leaves you exactly where you started unless you already had an assumption ready.
- **Asking everything up front.** Some questions belong later — ask about concurrent editors when you reach the data model, not in minute two.

## Key takeaways

- Six questions, each of which must be capable of changing the design.
- Device and network, the one thing that must feel instant, data size and churn, read vs write, concurrency, offline behaviour.
- Bundle questions and state your default so a shrug still moves you forward.
- Skip anything whose answer you would not act on.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Assume whatever you like."** — Then say your assumptions out loud and write them down. They become the contract you are judged against.
- **"Why does that matter?"** — Always have the answer ready: name the specific design fork the answer opens.

learnings.title: Scale math for frontends — budgets you can do in your head
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Interviewers at every tier listen for whether you quantify. You do not need precision — you need to reach "that's 4 MB, which is too much" out loud, in ten seconds, from numbers you carry around.

## Numbers worth memorising

| Quantity | Rule of thumb |
| --- | --- |
| 4G round trip | ~100 ms |
| 3G round trip | ~300 ms |
| 4G throughput (real, not spec) | ~1.5 MB/s |
| JS parse + compile | ~1 ms per KB on a mid-tier phone |
| One frame at 60 fps | 16.7 ms — of which you get ~10 |
| A "long task" | > 50 ms; anything longer is felt |
| Comfortable JS budget, mobile | ~170 KB compressed |
| One DOM node | ~1–2 KB of memory |
| A typical JSON list item | 0.5–2 KB |
| Human "instant" | < 100 ms |
| Human "still flowing" | < 1 s |
| Human "I've lost them" | > 10 s |

## The four calculations

### 1. Payload

> 20 feed items × 2 KB = 40 KB per page. Gzipped, roughly 12 KB. On 4G that is ~10 ms of transfer plus ~100 ms of round trip — the round trip dominates, so **fetching 20 at a time versus 40 barely matters; fetching twice does.**

That conclusion — latency dominates payload at these sizes — is the insight. It is why request *count* is usually the lever, not response size.

### 2. Bundle

> 700 KB of JS compressed is ~2.5 MB parsed. At ~1 ms/KB that is around 700 ms of main-thread parse and compile on a mid-range phone, before a single pixel. Plus ~500 ms of transfer on 4G. **We are 1.2 seconds in with nothing on screen.**

That is the argument for code splitting, made with arithmetic instead of adjectives.

### 3. DOM size

> 10,000 comments × ~8 nodes each = 80,000 nodes. At ~1.5 KB per node that is over 100 MB of memory, and style recalculation walks all of it. **Virtualization is not an optimisation here, it is a requirement** — render ~30 and recycle.

The threshold worth remembering: **above roughly 1,500–2,000 nodes, start worrying; above 10,000, virtualize.**

### 4. Update frequency

> 200 price ticks per second × 100 visible rows. If each tick re-renders its row, that is 200 renders/sec against a 60 fps budget — we are 3× over before React does anything. **Batch into animation frames and coalesce per row: at most 60 renders/sec, and usually far fewer because most rows do not change every frame.**

## Turning arithmetic into a design decision

The point is never the number; it is the fork the number opens.

| The arithmetic | The decision it forces |
| --- | --- |
| Round trip dominates payload | Merge endpoints or add a BFF; batch, don't shrink |
| 700 ms of parse before paint | Route-level code splitting, server render the shell |
| 80,000 DOM nodes | Virtualize, and cap what the API will return |
| 200 updates/sec | Coalesce into rAF, and subscribe per row, not per list |
| 3 sequential requests to paint | Parallelise, or move the join to the server |

## Doing it out loud

> "Let me sanity-check the size. A thread can hold 10,000 comments, each about 1 KB — that's 10 MB if we ever fetched it all, so we're paginating regardless. At 8 DOM nodes a comment, 10,000 of them is 80,000 nodes, which will blow out memory and style recalc. So: cursor pagination at 50 per page, and virtualize the rendered window. Both of those follow from the same number."

Ten seconds. Two architectural decisions, each justified by arithmetic rather than instinct.

## Common mistakes

- **Precision theatre.** Nobody wants 4 significant figures. Round aggressively and move.
- **Numbers with no conclusion.** Calculating 40 KB and then not saying what it means is worse than not calculating.
- **Desktop assumptions.** Budgets are set by the slowest device you support, not your laptop.
- **Forgetting parse cost.** Transfer is the visible half; parse and compile are the half that blocks the main thread.

## Key takeaways

- Carry ten rules of thumb; that is enough to reason about any frontend design.
- At typical payload sizes latency dominates, so request count is the lever.
- JS costs twice: transfer, then ~1 ms per KB of main-thread parse.
- Above ~10,000 DOM nodes, virtualization stops being optional.
- Always finish the arithmetic with the decision it forces.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Where did that number come from?"** — Say it is a rule of thumb and name the order of magnitude you trust it to. Honest approximation beats invented precision.
- **"What if the device is much slower?"** — Parse cost scales worst. The first lever is always shipping less JS, not optimising the JS you ship.

learnings.title: Defining success metrics — Core Web Vitals and what to add
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
A design with no success metric cannot be evaluated, only admired. Naming how you would *know* the design worked is a senior signal that costs one sentence. ## Core Web Vitals — the three that are standardised | Metric | Measures | Good (p75) | What breaks it | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **LCP** — Largest Contentful Paint | When the main content is visible | < 2.5 s | Slow server, render-blocking CSS/JS, unoptimised hero image, client-side data fetch before first paint | | **INP** — Interaction to Next Paint | Responsiveness across the whole visit | < 200 ms | Long tasks, heavy re-renders, synchronous work in handlers | | **CLS** — Cumulative Layout Shift | Visual stability | < 0.1 | Images without dimensions, injected banners, fonts swapping, content appearing above the viewport | INP replaced FID in 2024. FID only measured the *first* interaction's delay; INP measures the full interaction-to-paint latency across the session, so it is far harder to game and much closer to what people actually feel. **p75, not the average.** A quarter of your users having a bad time is a bad product, and averages hide exactly that. ## The ones vitals miss Vitals are about loading and responsiveness. They say nothing about whether your product works. | Metric | Why you need it | | --- | --- | | **TTFB** | Splits "server was slow" from "client was slow" — without it LCP regressions are unattributable | | **Time to first *meaningful* data** | LCP might be a skeleton. Track when the real content lands. | | **Custom "time to usable"** | For a dashboard, when the first chart is readable. Define it per product. | | **JS error rate per session** | The single best proxy for "is it broken" | | **Failed request rate, by endpoint** | Distinguishes your bug from their outage | | **Bundle size per route** | The leading indicator — it regresses weeks before LCP does | | **Long tasks per session** | The cause behind a bad INP | | **Interaction success rate** | Did the click actually accomplish the thing? | ## Lab versus field — and why you need both ```mermaid flowchart LR L["Lab (Lighthouse, CI)
same device, same network
catches regressions early
never matches reality"] --> D["Decide"] F["Field (RUM, CrUX)
real users, real devices
the actual truth
slow, noisy, post-hoc"] --> D ``` **Lab** is a controlled, repeatable number you can put in CI and block a PR on. It is not what your users experience. **Field** is what your users experience. It arrives days later and you cannot bisect it. Use lab to stop regressions landing; use field to decide what to work on. Saying that distinction out loud lands well: > "I'd gate PRs on a Lighthouse budget so regressions never merge, but I'd prioritise work from RUM — lab numbers on a fast machine will tell me everything is fine right up until it isn't." ## Wiring it up ```javascript import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS, onTTFB } from 'web-vitals'; function report({ name, value, rating, id }) { // sendBeacon survives the page being closed — fetch() often does not. navigator.sendBeacon( '/rum', JSON.stringify({ name, value, rating, // 'good' | 'needs-improvement' | 'poor' id, // groups metrics from one page visit route: location.pathname, release: __BUILD_SHA__, // so a regression points at a deploy conn: navigator.connection?.effectiveType, device: navigator.hardwareConcurrency, }), ); } onLCP(report); onINP(report); onCLS(report); onTTFB(report); ``` Three fields make this data actionable rather than decorative: **route** (so you know which screen), **release** (so a regression points at a deploy), and **connection/device** (so you can tell a slow site from a slow phone). ## Budgets, enforced A metric nobody enforces is a metric that drifts. Make it a build failure: ```json { "budgets": [{ "resourceSizes": [ { "resourceType": "script", "budget": 170 }, { "resourceType": "total", "budget": 500 } ], "timings": [{ "metric": "interactive", "budget": 3000 }] }] } ``` > "I'd put a bundle budget in CI. Not because 170 KB is magic, but because without a hard stop it grows one dependency at a time and nobody is ever responsible for the regression." ## Common mistakes - **Averages.** They hide the tail, and the tail is the problem. - **Lab only.** Your laptop on office wifi is not the user. - **Metrics with no owner and no threshold.** A dashboard nobody is accountable for changes nothing. - **Vitals only.** LCP can be perfect on a page whose primary action is broken. ## Key takeaways - LCP, INP, CLS at p75 — and INP replaced FID because it measures the whole visit. - Add TTFB, error rate, bundle size per route, and a product-specific "time to usable". - Lab gates regressions in CI; field decides priorities. - Tag every beacon with route, release and connection or the data is not actionable. - A budget only counts if it can fail a build. ## Interview follow-ups - **"LCP regressed 400 ms after a deploy. What now?"** — Split by TTFB first: if TTFB moved, it is the server; if not, look at what the deploy added to the critical path. - **"Which would you fix first, LCP or INP?"** — Depends on the product. A content site lives on LCP; an app people work in all day lives on INP.

learnings.title: Constraints that quietly change the whole design
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Some requirements are features. Others are constraints that propagate into every layer, and finding one late means redesigning. These are the ones worth surfacing in the first five minutes, because each of them is expensive to retrofit and cheap to design in.

## The six

### 1. The device floor

> "What is the slowest device we support?"

A mid-range Android from three years ago has roughly a **quarter** of the single-core performance of a current iPhone. Everything derived from the main thread — JS budget, hydration cost, animation strategy, whether virtualization is optional — is set by that device, not by your laptop.

If the answer is "it's an internal tool on company MacBooks", you have just been handed permission to skip a lot of work. Take it, and say so.

### 2. Network shape

Not just "slow" — **which kind of bad**:

| Shape | What it breaks | What it forces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High latency (satellite, rural) | Anything chatty | Batch requests, prefetch aggressively, merge endpoints |
| Low bandwidth | Large payloads and images | Aggressive compression, responsive images, pagination |
| Intermittent (transit, lifts) | Anything assuming a request completes | Offline reads, a durable write queue, idempotency |
| Metered | Video, prefetch, polling | Respect `saveData`, make prefetch opt-in |

### 3. Accessibility level

WCAG 2.1 **AA** is the usual bar, and in many jurisdictions a legal one for public services and large commerce. It is not a checklist you apply at the end — it constrains architecture:

- Custom dropdowns, modals and tabs need a **focus management design**, not a CSS class
- A virtualized list must keep the accessibility tree coherent while the DOM churns underneath it
- Live regions need to be designed, or a screen reader user learns nothing when content updates
- Colour choices are constrained by contrast before they are constrained by brand

> "I'd design the focus behaviour at the same time as the component API — where focus goes on open, where it returns on close, what's in the tab order. Retrofitting that onto a component tree that already exists is most of a rewrite."

### 4. Internationalisation

Cheap to design in, brutal to retrofit:

- **Text expands.** German runs 30–40% longer than English; fixed-width buttons break.
- **RTL is not a stylesheet.** Layout mirrors, icons flip (but not all of them — a play button never mirrors), and logical CSS properties (`margin-inline-start`) stop being a nicety.
- **Pluralisation is not `n === 1`.** Arabic has six plural forms, Polish three. Use ICU message format, never string concatenation.
- **Dates, numbers, currency, collation** all belong to `Intl`, not to hand-rolled formatting.
- **Locale bundles** are a code-splitting problem: ship one locale, not forty.

### 5. Regulatory and privacy

- **GDPR / CCPA** — consent before non-essential cookies and analytics, which means your analytics cannot load on first paint and your "accept all" banner is now on the critical path.
- **Data residency** — may dictate which CDN regions and which error-tracking vendor.
- **PCI** — card fields belong in a hosted iframe you do not control, which constrains your checkout component design.
- **Healthcare / finance** — audit logging, session timeout, and often a hard no on session replay.

These sound like someone else's problem right up until "the cookie banner must block analytics" lands in your LCP.

### 6. The team and the calendar

The constraint candidates never mention, and the one that decides real architectures:

> "Micro-frontends solve deploy coupling between teams. With three teams in one repo, they cost you a shared design system, a routing contract, and roughly one engineer full-time to maintain the shell. I'd stay in a monorepo with clear ownership boundaries until there are five or six teams, or until deploy coordination is genuinely the bottleneck."

Naming an architecture's *organisational* price is a Staff-level move.

## Surfacing them

You cannot ask six questions about constraints and still have time to design. Bundle them:

> "Before I start — anything unusual about devices, network, accessibility level, or locales? I'll assume mid-range Android on 4G, WCAG AA, and English-only unless you tell me otherwise. Any of those being different would change the design quite a bit."

One sentence, and you have both covered the constraint space and set defaults.

## Common mistakes

- **Treating a11y and i18n as polish.** Both are structural; both are far more expensive later.
- **Designing for your own device.** The floor is set by the worst supported device.
- **Missing the consent banner's cost.** It is often the single largest thing on the critical path.
- **Ignoring team shape.** Architecture that does not fit the org chart does not survive contact with it.

## Key takeaways

- Device floor sets the JS and main-thread budget; your laptop is not the target.
- "Bad network" has four distinct shapes and each forces a different mitigation.
- WCAG AA constrains component architecture, not just styling.
- i18n means text expansion, true RTL, ICU plurals, `Intl`, and per-locale bundles.
- Team count and deploy coupling are real architectural constraints — price them.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"We only support modern browsers."** — Ask what modern means. Safari's release cadence is tied to iOS versions, and it is usually the real constraint.
- **"How much does accessibility cost?"** — Roughly nothing when designed in, roughly a rewrite when retrofitted. That contrast is the answer.
